newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Israel under fire at U.N. over tunnel, peace delay.
newsitem.headline: Israel under fire at U.N. over tunnel, peace delay.

text.p: Israel came under sustained fire in the Security Council on Friday over an archaeological tunnel in the Old City of Jerusalem and delays in the Middle East peace process.
Speaker after speaker called for the closing of the tunnel, which passes near the al-Aqsa mosque, Islam's third-holiest shrine, and warned that the peace process risked collapse.
Israel rejected what it called the "distortions of fact ... regarding the dramatic events ... which have cast such a dark cloud over the entire peace process."

More than 50 Palestinians and more than a dozen Israelis have been killed and hundreds have been wounded in the latest violence. It erupted after Israel opened a new entrance to an underground passage along the Western, or Wailing, Wall, intended as a window on 2,500 years of history.

Farouk Kaddoumi, who heads the Palestine Liberation Organisation's political department, said the violence resulted from "an accumulation of simmering tensions" for which Israel alone bore full responsibility.

He cited a long list of actions by Israel's new right-wing government, led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, including the resumption of settlement activities, confiscation of Arab land, destruction of a community centre in East Jerusalem, failure to withdraw from the West Bank town of Hebron and sealing of the occupied territories.
If Israel's "brutal measures" continue, the Middle East peace process will be "in mortal peril," Kaddoumi said.
"These require denunciation from this council and a demand that Israel put an end to its provocative acts and close the tunnel in order to defuse the escalating tensions," he said.
"We recommend that this council dispatch a fact-finding mission and call for peace in the occupied territories and examine in full detail the situation there."

Israeli Foreign Minister David Levy rejected what he called the "orchestrated attempt to place blame on Israel and to portray her as the sole responsible party for the bitter harvest of blood" in which Palestinians and Israelis had died.

"I come to refute in their entirety the distortions of fact which are being spread here regarding the dramatic events of the last days and which have cast such a dark cloud over the entire peace process," he said.
Whatever claims are made against Israel, they do not justify the "incitement to violence and the use of live weapons," he said.

"The atmosphere of escalation and the threats and the calls for armed struggle will not move us from the fundamental principles which guide our policy: the pursuit of peace while ensuring national and personal security for our citizens."
The tunnel has no religious significance and the issue is being manipulated, Levy said, adding that Israel has safeguarded the freedom of worship of all faiths.
The debate was marked by the participation of a number of foreign ministers who are in New York for the U.N. General Assembly.
Egyptian Foreign Minister Amre Moussa accused Israel of "shameful stalling" over the peace process and called on it to implement agreements already made with the Palestinians.
"I call upon the Israeli government to reconsider its policy," he said, adding, "The alternative to peace is something that the international community cannot bear."

British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind called for a moratorium on opening the tunnel, which Israel announced on Friday had been temporarily closed. Like many other speakers, he urged a meeting between Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov accused Israel of stalling in the Middle East peace process and said the latest crisis was a "direct result of reckless activity."

French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette also criticised Israel and called for closing of the tunnel. The peace process was "in danger of seeing its death knell if the international community does not act quickly and firmly," he said.
